doc.title: Doug Carn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 24, 2023

title: Artistic vision, regrets, weddings and suffering
summary: Carn would not do it all the same again, defends playing weddings, and rejects the idea that musicians must suffer.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: Do you think you made decisions along your career that cost you money but you stuck with your artistic vision?

Yeah. I hate to see those interviews, they say well look, just tell me if you had to do it all over again would you do the same thing? They said well yeah, really you know, I’d do the same thing. But I wouldn’t. You know? If I know what I know now, I wouldn’t do the same thing you know. But they don’t want to admit that they weren’t perfect, or they still want to imagine that life was idealized for them. No if I had to do the same thing over again I wouldn’t do it the same way. Hell no.

I’m always surprised when I learn about musicians that I listened to and read about when — growing up, and in some cases I got to meet them and to find out that they would play gigs that I would never imagine. That they would play weddings, you know, because everybody’s got to make a buck.

Right. And then too, I’m going to tell you all this truth, man — it’s nothing wrong with playing a wedding. I played a wedding in 2012 with the same band I had in Dizzy’s Coca Cola, because the guy was a friend of mine and he was a fan of mine and he loved jazz you know, and he wanted a real jazz group at his daughter’s wedding. You know? So we played it you know? But what’s wrong with playing a miscellaneous wedding for miscellaneous people for miscellaneous money on a miscellaneous circumstance. But a good wedding like Oscar Peterson played for Prince Charles’ and Diana’s wedding, or the reception. I would have played that gig in a minute. You know I played for weddings, © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
I played for a funeral, I played for a birthday party, but the real deal, not no jive, this poverty-stricken, you know, and academically deplete you know, depleted or whatever you know.

Sometimes — I think the public, I think the public is fascinated sometimes with the struggle of musicians and they think it’s a royal thing to do to stick to your musical vision and live in poverty for it.

Yeah. Well that’s the western point of view anyway. That’s one of the things I don’t like about some people interpreting Christianity. They thing you’re supposed to suffer you know. You ain’t supposed to suffer, you know, and a lot of times they won’t get you a good hotel room or get you good food, because the harder it is, you know, to be out there, the better you play. I say I’ll play better when I get a limo then a suite you know, in a five-star building.
